Anthony Gatto says he has been training since he was 3 years old and performing since he was 8. In the performers’ tent for the touring show “Kooza,” chiseled men catapult their partners onto one another’s shoulders from a giant seesaw, while a woman contorts herself atop child-sized blocks. There is only so much of this a person can take before the ego begins craving something normal.

Normal might appear to be the man in the corner, wearing a T-shirt, shorts and sneakers, casually tossing balls into the air. How hard can that be?

Your self-worth is quickly dashed again when he picks up a soccer ball, bounces it on his head and jumps rope at the same time. Moments later, he is juggling six or seven orange rings—moving so quickly they blur—then performs a pirouette while all the rings are in the air before catching them on his arm.

Watch the juggler in action »

You could say Anthony Gatto went into the family business. But his stepfather was not a farmer or a doctor. He was a juggler.

“By the time I was 8, I was entered into a juggling competition, and incidentally, that was the same competition that Patrick Dempsey, the actor, was in,” Gatto said. “He used to be a juggler. We competed against each other. I took first, he took second. Now he’s a big actor and here I am, juggling.”

Gatto is being modest. In fact, he did not audition for “Kooza.” The show sought him out.

“I have right now 11 juggling world records,” he said. “Some of them I’ve held since I was 16 years old and they have yet to be beaten.”

Imagine a wearable disco ball. That is not far from the form-fitting costume Gatto wears onstage. Backstage, he is in a long-sleeve T-shirt, gym shorts and sneakers. But there is nothing casual about his daily routine. He typically works out and practices six to seven hours a day to prepare for his 10 minutes in the spotlight. In fact, he continues practicing until moments before he runs onstage.

“Juggling is something that is so delicate, you have to have a really good feel, you can lose that in minutes,” he said. “There are so many variables that can affect you. If it’s a humid day, it’s a very difficult task to get through the number that I do. The wind, if there’s any air current in there and you’re expecting to catch a ring and it blows an inch, you miss it.”

But he rarely misses—at least not during his act.

This performer, who depends on coordination and concentration for 350 shows a year, admits that his most embarrassing moments have nothing to do with balls, clubs or rings. It is acting that trips him up.

“I have fallen as the delivery-man character in the show. In fact, I have done this a few times,” he said. “I like to think it’s because I put my heart and soul into the characters I’m portraying.”

Surrounded by so much talent and precision, there is some comfort in knowing that one of the best—perhaps the best juggler in the world—is also a klutz.

(CNN) — A trip behind the scenes at Cirque du Soleil is not recommended if you want to feel good about yourself.

Anthony Gatto says he began training when he was just 3 and was already performing by age 8. Inside the performers’ tent for the touring production “Kooza,” muscular acrobats launch partners from an enormous teeterboard onto one another’s shoulders, while a female performer twists her body into extreme positions atop blocks sized for children. After seeing enough of that, you may find yourself searching for something more ordinary to restore your confidence.

That “ordinary” sight might appear to be a man off to the side in a T-shirt, shorts and sneakers, tossing balls into the air. How difficult could that possibly be?

Any remaining self-assurance disappears almost immediately when he grabs a soccer ball, balances and bounces it on his head, and skips rope at the same time. Soon afterward, he is juggling six or seven orange rings — moving so quickly they seem to smear into a blur — then spins in a pirouette while every ring is airborne before catching them on his arm.

You could describe Gatto’s career as joining the family trade. His stepfather, however, was not a farmer or physician. He was a juggler.

“By the time I was 8, I was entered into a juggling competition, and incidentally, that was the same competition that Patrick Dempsey, the actor, was in,” Gatto said. “He used to be a juggler. We competed against each other. I took first, he took second. Now he’s a big actor and here I am, juggling.”

Gatto understates his accomplishments. He did not try out for “Kooza”; instead, the production sought him out.

“I have right now 11 juggling world records,” he said. “Some of them I’ve held since I was 16 years old and they have yet to be beaten.”

Onstage, Gatto wears a tight costume that could almost be compared to a disco ball made into clothing. Offstage, he switches to a long-sleeved T-shirt, athletic shorts and sneakers. His schedule, though, is anything but relaxed. To be ready for the 10 minutes he spends in front of the audience, he usually trains and rehearses six to seven hours each day. He continues practicing until just before he goes on.

“Juggling is something that is so delicate, you have to have a really good feel, you can lose that in minutes,” he said. “There are so many variables that can affect you. If it’s a humid day, it’s a very difficult task to get through the number that I do. The wind, if there’s any air current in there and you’re expecting to catch a ring and it blows an inch, you miss it.”

Even so, he almost never misses during his routine. The performer, whose work depends on precision, coordination and intense focus for 350 shows each year, says his most embarrassing mishaps have not involved balls, clubs or rings. Instead, acting has caused the trouble.

“I have fallen as the delivery-man character in the show. In fact, I have done this a few times,” he said. “I like to think it’s because I put my heart and soul into the characters I’m portraying.”

In the middle of so much extraordinary skill and accuracy, it is oddly reassuring to learn that one of the world’s greatest jugglers — perhaps the greatest — can also be clumsy.

Balls, rings, clubs — they rise, fall, cross, vanish, return. His hands move with the calm efficiency of a man sorting mail, except the mail is airborne and arriving in several dimensions at once. Watching Gatto juggle is to confront an uncomfortable truth: Some people are born with gifts, and some of us still drop our keys while standing still.

In “Kooza,” Cirque du Soleil’s high-wire valentine to old-school circus thrills, Gatto’s act is both deceptively simple and technically outrageous. There are no explosions, no digital effects, no elaborate narrative to decode. Just a man, a stage and the kind of coordination that makes audience members involuntarily mutter, “How?”

That question has followed Gatto for most of his life. A juggling prodigy, he was performing before many children have mastered tying their shoes. By adulthood, he had become one of the most celebrated jugglers in the world, known not only for speed and precision but for a rare ability to make the impossible appear almost relaxed.

Almost.

The trick with Gatto is that he does not sell effort. He does not grimace through the hard parts or pause theatrically to announce that something difficult is about to happen. Instead, he glides into escalating patterns with the unbothered expression of someone waiting for coffee. Seven balls? Fine. A blur of clubs? Certainly. Rings slicing through the air like neon halos? Why not.

That deadpan control is part of the pleasure. Cirque du Soleil can overwhelm the senses with its costumes, lighting, music and elastic human architecture, but Gatto’s performance draws power from clarity. The audience knows exactly what is at stake: things are in the air, and they must not fall.

Of course, in the hands of a master, “not falling” becomes a whole philosophy.

“Kooza” itself is a return to circus fundamentals — acrobatics, clowning, danger, spectacle — wrapped in Cirque’s surreal visual language. The show follows the Innocent, a wide-eyed character pulled into a strange world populated by kings, tricksters and daredevils. Around him, performers launch themselves onto teeterboards, soar through the air and tempt fate on the Wheel of Death, a rotating apparatus that appears to have been designed by someone who thought treadmills needed more menace.

Within that carnival of nerve, Gatto’s juggling serves as a reminder that virtuosity does not always need height or fire. Sometimes the most astonishing thing in the room is focus.

Backstage, that focus is everywhere. Cirque performers inhabit a strange middle ground between athlete, actor and mythological creature. They tape ankles, rehearse cues, apply elaborate makeup and prepare to do nightly what most people would consider a medical emergency. The atmosphere is part locker room, part theater, part international airport lounge for people with extraordinary core strength.

Gatto fits comfortably into that ecosystem, though his act stands apart because of its clean geometry. Juggling is ancient entertainment, but at his level it becomes nearly mathematical — arcs, timing, rotation, velocity. The comedy is that the viewer’s brain understands the basic concept instantly and then spends the rest of the act failing to process the execution.

One object goes up. Another comes down. The hands alternate. Easy.

Then the pattern multiplies until it seems less like a person juggling and more like weather forming around him.

That is what makes Gatto such a strong match for “Kooza.” The show celebrates the human body under pressure: balancing, flying, bending, risking. His pressure is measured in fractions of seconds. A throw slightly too high, a hand a whisper too late, a club spinning off-axis — any small betrayal could break the spell. The thrill is not that the audience expects him to fail. It is that success looks so improbable, so repeatedly.

And yet there he is, night after night, making chaos behave.

There is a special indignity in watching someone do something impossibly hard while appearing serene. It leaves the rest of us exposed. We remember the time we tried to juggle three oranges in a kitchen and ended up apologizing to the fruit bowl. We consider our own hand-eye coordination and find it wanting. We wonder whether it is too late to develop a marketable skill beyond “typing while anxious.”

But that, ultimately, is the joy of Cirque du Soleil. It is not there to make normal people feel athletic. It is there to make the human possible seem larger than we remembered.

Backstage at “Kooza,” among the contortionists, acrobats, clowns and daredevils, self-esteem may take a temporary hit. But out front, under the lights, that feeling turns into something better: awe.

And when Anthony Gatto sends another impossible constellation spinning through the air, the only reasonable response is to sit very still, keep both feet safely on the floor and applaud the man who has clearly made a private arrangement with gravity.

# The Ten-Minute Miracle: Inside the Daily Grind of a Cirque du Soleil Juggler

By the time the audience sees him, he looks effortless.

Under the lights, with music swelling and the stage alive around him, the Cirque du Soleil juggler steps into a world of impossible timing. Balls, clubs, or rings carve bright arcs through the air. His hands move with machine-like precision, but his face stays calm, almost playful. For 10 minutes, he seems to bend gravity into choreography.

What the audience does not see is the six to seven hours of daily practice that make those 10 minutes possible.

For an elite juggler in Cirque du Soleil, the performance is only the tip of the spear. The real work happens long before showtime, in rehearsal rooms, backstage spaces, and quiet corners where the same throw is repeated hundreds—sometimes thousands—of times until the body no longer has to ask the mind what comes next.

“People think the hard part is the show,” he says with a laugh. “But the show is what happens after all the hard parts.”

## A Workday Measured in Throws

His practice schedule is closer to that of an Olympic athlete than a traditional stage performer. A typical day may begin with conditioning: shoulders, wrists, core, legs. Juggling looks like it belongs mostly to the hands, but at the highest level, the whole body is involved. Balance, posture, breathing, and endurance all matter.

Then come drills.

He breaks his practice into sections: technique, accuracy, speed, recovery, and performance consistency. One hour might be devoted to clean patterns. Another to difficult transitions. Another to correcting tiny mistakes that most spectators would never notice: a throw drifting slightly too far forward, a catch landing in the wrong part of the hand, a pause that disrupts the rhythm of the act.

Six or seven hours of practice does not mean nonstop tossing. It means a disciplined cycle of repetition, rest, adjustment, and repetition again. He films himself. He studies angles. He counts drops. He practices not only success, but failure—how to recover when a prop slips, when a hand is late, when the stage picture changes unexpectedly.

Because in Cirque du Soleil, juggling is not simply juggling. It is theater, acrobatics, music, lighting, costume, and character all fused into one brief, unforgiving window.

## The Pressure of 10 Minutes

His stage act lasts about 10 minutes. That may sound short, but in performance terms, it is an eternity.

For those 10 minutes, there is no room for distraction. Every throw must arrive on time. Every movement must fit the score. Every facial expression must serve the story. The juggler is not standing alone at a street corner or in a practice studio; he is part of a living machine of performers, technicians, riggers, musicians, and stage managers.

A missed catch is not just a missed catch. It can affect spacing, timing, and the emotional rhythm of the scene.

“That’s the funny thing,” he says. “You practice all day so that, for 10 minutes, it looks like you’re not trying.”

The goal is not to show effort. It is to create wonder.

That means the technical demands are hidden beneath style. A trick that took months to perfect might flash by in seconds. A transition that required endless drilling might be invisible to the audience. If he does his job perfectly, spectators do not think about the mechanics. They simply gasp.

## Weather, the Invisible Opponent

Even the best jugglers must answer to the air.

Humidity and wind can transform a familiar routine into a dangerous puzzle. In an indoor theater, conditions are carefully controlled. But touring, rehearsal spaces, outdoor events, and backstage environments can introduce variables that matter deeply to a juggler.

Humidity changes grip. A prop that feels smooth and predictable in dry air may become tacky or slippery when moisture rises. Skin reacts too. Hands sweat differently. Tape, resin, costume fabric, and prop surfaces can all behave in slightly altered ways.

For a casual observer, these differences might seem microscopic. For a professional juggler, they are enormous.

“When you’re throwing something high, even a small change matters,” he explains. “You feel it immediately.”

Wind is worse. A light breeze can push a ring off course. Clubs, with their rotating shape, may become unstable. Even balls can drift if thrown high enough. The juggler must adjust instantly: lower the pattern, change the force of the throw, alter body position, or compensate with footwork.

Wind is not just physical. It is psychological. It introduces uncertainty into an art built on precision.

“You learn to listen to the air,” he says. “That sounds poetic, but it’s true. You can feel when the space is different.”

## Precision Meets Personality

Technical mastery, however, is only part of the job. In Cirque du Soleil, performers are expected to become characters. They are not merely demonstrating skill; they are telling a story.

This is where the juggler admits, with charming honesty, that he sometimes struggles.

“I can juggle complicated patterns,” he says, grinning. “But when they ask me to act clumsy, I become actually clumsy.”

It is a wonderfully human confession from someone whose career depends on coordination. Onstage, comic timing can be just as difficult as a seven-object pattern. Pretending to stumble without truly losing control requires a different kind of precision. The body must appear awkward while remaining completely safe. A fake trip must land exactly on the beat. A comic pause must last long enough to earn a laugh, but not so long that it disrupts the act.

For a performer trained to eliminate mistakes, acting messy can feel unnatural.

“When I’m juggling, I know what to do,” he says. “When I’m acting, suddenly I don’t know where my arms are.”

That contrast—between elite control and playful vulnerability—is part of what makes his performance memorable. The audience sees not just skill, but personality. He is not a machine. He is a person negotiating risk, comedy, and beauty in real time.

## The Art of Making Difficulty Disappear

The magic of Cirque du Soleil has always depended on contradiction. Performers must be superhuman and relatable, precise and spontaneous, disciplined and free. The juggler’s 10-minute act is a perfect example.

Behind it are years of training and hours of daily work. There are sore wrists, bruised fingers, frustrating rehearsals, and tiny technical corrections repeated until they become instinct. There are battles with humidity, wind, lighting, costume restrictions, and the unforgiving physics of objects in flight.

And then, when the curtain rises, all of that disappears.

What remains is wonder: a figure under the lights, tossing impossible shapes into the air and catching them as if gravity has agreed to cooperate.

For 10 minutes, he gives the audience a miracle.

For six or seven hours a day, he earns it.
